My point estimates reflect a relatively stable baseline with modest upward drift across horizons. At the one-day horizon, I anchored heavily on the most recent observed price or level, assuming minimal overnight movement and treating the near-term as essentially locked in — hence the tight interval collapsing to the point estimate itself. The one-month estimate extends that drift further, arriving at 72.0, which represents a continuation of the same gentle upward trajectory without assuming any major structural break.

The confidence interval widths expand substantially as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the standard statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the interval is essentially degenerate because very short-term price or value changes tend to be small relative to the precision of the estimate. By one week, the 90% interval spans roughly 17.5 units (63.0 to 80.5), capturing plausible weekly volatility. By one month, the interval widens to about 30.5 units (57.5 to 88.0), reflecting that a full month allows for meaningful trend reversals, external shocks, or regime changes that simply cannot materialize within a single trading day.

Sentiment shifts, liquidity conditions, and correlated market movements can all amplify or dampen realized volatility well beyond historical averages. The width of my intervals was calibrated using something like historical volatility or analogous reference-class data, but that calibration assumes the near future resembles the recent past in terms of volatility regime.

There are plausible tail risks that could push outcomes outside even the stated 90% intervals. A sudden policy shock — central bank surprise, geopolitical escalation, or a major data surprise — could easily generate moves exceeding the interval bounds in either direction. On the upside, a strong catalyst or short-squeeze dynamic could push well above 88.0 within a month. On the downside, a risk-off episode or structural negative development could drive the value below 57.5. These scenarios are unlikely by construction (they sit in the outer 10% of my distribution), but they are by no means implausible given how frequently tail events occur in financial and economic contexts.
